uncited: Anti-aliasing techniques for splatting address the sample-rate aliasing artifacts (pre-aliasing) that occur when the integration grid sampling frequency is insufficient relative to the volume raster during the resampling phase .

Unlike volume ray-casting, which performs reconstruction in eye space and naturally adapts kernel size as rays diverge, splatting performs reconstruction in perspective space, requiring explicit mechanisms to maintain the Nyquist criterion .

These methods distinguish themselves from sibling techniques by either dynamically scaling splat size and energy for distant voxels [4471-anti-aliasing-for-splatting.md], or by hybridizing polygonal slicing with ellipsoidal splats to handle geometric detail and low-density regions simultaneously [829-splatting-for-anti-aliasing-small-cells.md][1447-threshold-slicing-and-anti-aliasing.md].
Each primitive $k$ is defined by its position $\mathbf{p}_k$, density/extinction coefficient $g_k$ or $\rho_k$, and a reconstruction kernel $h$ (typically a Gaussian) .
**Transformation:** Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., shear-warp) .
For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., EWA splatting) to account for foreshortening .
This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly .
Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time) .
**Hardware Acceleration:** Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity .
The problem of aliasing in volume rendering, particularly during resampling, was formally addressed in the context of splatting by Westover .

The distinction between eye-space reconstruction (ray casting) and perspective-space reconstruction (splatting) highlights the unique challenges of maintaining the Nyquist criterion in splatting-based pipelines .

Subsequent developments introduced hybrid approaches combining polygonal slicing with splatting to handle unstructured grids and adaptive meshes, such as those by Kindlmann and Westover  and later refinements by others .
